changes.summary: The Ancient Mediterranean holdings at the Menil Collection number more than 600 objects and span 20,000 years of artistic achievement, from the Upper Paleolithic era (ca. 10,000 BCE or earlier) to the end of the Roman Empire (4th century CE). The rotating displays highlight ancient visual cultures from the islands of the Mediterranean Sea and surrounding regions of Europe, North Africa, and western Asia. The gallery welcomes visitors with a display of important Cycladic figures, a snarling Etruscan winged feline, and painted Greek drinking vessels. One side of the gallery flows into the eastern Mediterranean with examples associated with the ancient civilizations of Cyprus, Turkey, and the Mesopotamian kingdoms of Sumer and Babylonia in present day Iraq. On the opposite side, a sunken relief featuring the god Horus (1295–1186 BCE) punctuates the presentation of works from Ancient Egypt, which opens into the museum’s galleries of African art. A 2nd-century BCE Carthaginian coin and a small copper-alloy falcon head, a fragment from an 8th–6th century BCE statue of Horus, are among the earliest antiquities acquired by John and Dominique de Menil. They assembled the majority of the museum’s ancient Mediterranean objects between the 1950s and 1970s, concurrent with their educational exhibition-making initiatives at local universities. Representations of Black Africans in antiquity are a significant theme in the museum’s collection, reflecting the focus developed in concert with the research project The Image of the Black in Western Art. In the mid-1960s, the development of the exhibition Ten Centuries that Shaped the West: Greek and Roman Art in Texas Collections proved to be a principal motivator for acquiring works from the ancient Mediterranean.
